author: A Robot

modules.description: Students explore the gross anatomy of the heart, identifying the four chambers and major vessels entering and leaving the heart. The heart is presented in anatomical position and rotated to allow examination from multiple angles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart (right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle)
Locate the major vessels entering and leaving the heart (superior and inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries and veins, aorta)
Distinguish structural differences between atria and ventricles
instructions: Observe the 3D model of the heart as it rotates in anatomical position
Listen carefully as each chamber and major vessel is identified and labeled
Notice the relative thickness of the left and right ventricles
Use your pointer to examine different parts of the heart as they are highlighted

clips.changeMeaning: Introduction and initial display of the rotating heart model to establish anatomical orientation and prepare students for structural identification
clips.narration: Welcome to the anatomy of the human heart. The heart is a muscular, four-chambered organ that pumps blood throughout the body. In this module, we will examine the structure of the heart, including its four chambers and the major blood vessels that connect to it. The heart is shown here in anatomical position, with the apex pointing downward and to the left. Notice how the organ rotates slowly so you can observe it from all angles.

clips.changeMeaning: Camera position shifts to highlight the four chambers and introduce the concept of differential wall thickness between ventricles
clips.narration: The heart consists of four chambers: two atria and two ventricles. The right atrium and left atrium are the smaller, thin-walled upper chambers that receive blood. The right ventricle and left ventricle are the larger, muscular lower chambers that pump blood out of the heart. Notice that the left ventricle has a noticeably thicker myocardium—the muscle layer—than the right ventricle. We will explore why this difference exists later.

clips.changeMeaning: Major vessels are now visible and labeled as the heart model is rotated to show anterior and lateral views for optimal vessel visibility
clips.narration: Now let's identify the major blood vessels connected to the heart. The superior and inferior vena cava bring deoxygenated blood from the body into the right atrium. The pulmonary arteries carry blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. The pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Finally, the aorta is the largest artery in the body, carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the systemic circulation. These six major vessels are the main entry and exit points for blood flow through the heart.

modules.description: Students learn about the four heart valves, their location, and their role in preventing backflow. An interactive animated model shows the valves opening and closing during the cardiac cycle.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the location of the four heart valves (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral/bicuspid, aortic)
Understand the distinction between atrioventricular valves and semilunar valves
Comprehend how valves prevent backflow of blood during the cardiac cycle
instructions: Watch as each valve is identified in the heart model
Observe the valve animation showing opening and closing during the cardiac cycle
Notice which valves prevent blood from flowing backward between specific chambers and vessels

clips.changeMeaning: Introduction to valve types and classification, with the heart model positioned to show the valve locations in cross-section
clips.narration: The heart contains four valves that are essential for one-way blood flow. These valves open and close in a coordinated pattern during each heartbeat to ensure blood moves in the correct direction and doesn't flow backward. There are two types of valves: the atrioventricular valves, which separate the atria from the ventricles, and the semilunar valves, which separate the ventricles from the arteries.

clips.changeMeaning: Heart model rotates to highlight the atrioventricular valves; valve indicators are enabled and highlighted with color
clips.narration: The atrioventricular valves are the tricuspid valve and the mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve. The tricuspid valve, located between the right atrium and right ventricle, has three cusps or leaflets. The mitral valve, located between the left atrium and left ventricle, has two cusps. During atrial contraction, these valves open to allow blood to flow from the atria into the ventricles. When the ventricles contract, these valves close to prevent blood from flowing backward into the atria.

clips.changeMeaning: Heart model continues rotation; focus shifts to the semilunar valves and their asymmetric pressure demands
clips.narration: The semilunar valves are the pulmonary valve and the aortic valve. The pulmonary valve separates the right ventricle from the pulmonary arteries. The aortic valve separates the left ventricle from the aorta. These crescent-shaped valves open when the ventricles contract, allowing blood to be ejected into the arteries. They close immediately after to prevent blood from flowing backward into the ventricles during the filling phase. The aortic valve tends to be stronger and thicker than the pulmonary valve because it must withstand greater pressure from the powerful left ventricle.

modules.moduleName: Blood Flow Through the Heart: The Dual Circulation
modules.description: Students trace the complete path of blood through the heart's dual circulation system. An animated pathway shows deoxygenated blood entering from the body, being pumped to the lungs (pulmonary circuit), then returning oxygenated blood to be distributed throughout the body (systemic circuit).
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the complete pathway of blood through the heart and lungs (pulmonary circulation)
Trace the role of the heart in systemic circulation
Explain the sequence of chambers and valves blood passes through in a complete circulation cycle
Connect the dual circulation concept to the functional specialization of the right and left heart
instructions: Follow the animated blood flow pathway as it is traced through the heart
Identify each chamber and valve in the sequence
Observe how blood changes color to indicate oxygenation status
Understand the two distinct circuits: pulmonary and systemic

clips.changeMeaning: Introduction to dual circulation concept with both blood flow pathways labeled and color-coded on either side of the heart model
clips.narration: The heart drives two interconnected circulatory pathways simultaneously. In the pulmonary circuit, deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right heart and is pumped to the lungs for oxygen exchange. In the systemic circuit, oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the left heart and is pumped out to supply the entire body. Both circuits operate with each heartbeat. Let's trace the path of blood through each circuit step by step.

clips.changeMeaning: The deoxygenated blood pathway is highlighted as it flows from vena cava through the right heart to the pulmonary arteries
clips.narration: Deoxygenated blood returns from the body through the superior and inferior vena cava and enters the right atrium. The right atrium contracts, and blood flows through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle then contracts, pushing blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries, which carry this deoxygenated blood to the lungs. In the lungs, blood releases carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen.

clips.changeMeaning: The oxygenated blood pathway is now highlighted flowing from the lungs through the left heart to the aorta; the contrast between ventricle wall thickness becomes evident
clips.narration: After exchanging gases in the lungs, oxygenated blood returns via the pulmonary veins and enters the left atrium. The left atrium contracts, and blood flows through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. The left ventricle is the most muscular chamber because it must generate enough force to pump oxygenated blood through the aortic valve and into the aorta, which distributes it throughout the entire body. This systemic circulation delivers oxygen to all tissues and organs.

clips.changeMeaning: Heart model is rotated and scaled to emphasize the dramatic difference in ventricular wall thickness, completing the explanation of structure-function relationship
clips.narration: You may have noticed that the left ventricle has a much thicker myocardium than the right ventricle. This structural difference directly reflects the functional demands of each ventricle. The right ventricle only needs to pump blood through the lungs, which are in close proximity and have relatively low vascular resistance. The left ventricle, however, must generate sufficient pressure to push blood through the entire systemic circulation to all parts of the body against much higher vascular resistance. This greater workload requires a thicker, more muscular left ventricular wall. Typically, the left ventricular wall is two to three times thicker than the right ventricular wall.
